items.anchor_quote: Although no single reference aerosol can be used to simulate the response
items.summary: Ground study testing whether laboratory reference aerosols can act as transfer standards for spacecraft smoke detector testing. Mineral oil (Gemini 501B tester) and DOS (atomizer, 1.5-100% solutions) together spanned the detector-response range of six smokes from oxidative pyrolysis of spacecraft-relevant materials, but no single reference aerosol reproduced the response of the different detection technologies to the different smokes within +/-10%; the derived reference-to-smoke relationships are proposed as conversion factors.

numbers.meaning: accuracy target that no single reference aerosol met across detectors and smokes

items.scope_notes: Applies to ground tube-furnace oxidative pyrolysis smokes in a 326-L chamber, not flaming fires, not low gravity. Concentration reference is the DustTrak DRX PM2.5 reading, itself size/composition dependent.

verification.note: Anchor on p.1. Summary, +/-10% and test scope match the abstract and conclusion (p.11).

items.anchor_quote: Although there is no established standard for spacecraft smoke detectors
items.summary: The authors note that, unlike consumer alarms regulated by UL 217, there is no established performance standard for spacecraft smoke detectors; they are tested with methods similar to UL 217 but using fuels representative of spacecraft materials.
items.scope_notes: Statement about the standards landscape as of 2020; see HALO 2025 paper for a later restatement.

items.location: Sec. II.A Experimental Setup (pp.2-3; 326-L chamber and tube furnace on p.2, detectors/DRX/4.4 L/min on p.3)
items.anchor_quote: A Commercial Space Prototype (CSP) smoke detector based on light scattering was co-located
items.summary: Experiments in the GASP laboratory at NASA GRC: reference or smoke aerosols were injected into a 326-L mixed chamber. A light-scattering Commercial Space Prototype (CSP) detector and a commercial ionization detector (IonZG) were logged at 10 Hz; two Kidde consumer alarms (ionization and photoelectric) were logged only as alarm state; a second sample line fed the ISS light-scattering detector and the STS ionization detector, which have no pump and were drawn by a fan. A DustTrak DRX (655 nm laser scattering) served as concentration reference, plus an ASTM E662 obscuration meter; smoke came from a tube furnace flushed with 4.4 L/min filtered air.

numbers.meaning: size below which high-concentration monodisperse DOS was difficult

items.location: Sec. II.C Smoke Aerosol Materials (continues p.5)
items.anchor_quote: Six types of materials relevant to spacecraft safety were tested
items.summary: Smoke was generated by oxidative pyrolysis of six spacecraft-relevant materials in a tube furnace: cotton lamp wick (3 tests, 0.75-1 g, 200-240 C), Kapton (3 tests, 1-2 g, 450-500 C), Nomex (3 tests, 0.5-1 g, 350-400 C), Teflon/PTFE (3 tests, about 8 g, 400-500 C), PMMA (1 test, 2 g, 200 C) and fluoropolymer/polyimide wire insulation (1 test, 2 g, 450 C).
items.scope_notes: (i) Kapton and Teflon smokes are included. Smoldering/oxidative pyrolysis only (no flaming); 1-3 tests per material, PMMA and wire insulation single tests.

items.summary: With mineral-oil reference aerosol, the ISS light-scattering detector signal rose linearly to about 4 V at about 50 mg/m3 (DRX PM2.5) and saturated at about 6 V above roughly 70 mg/m3; its data from one of the three test days were invalidated by a transfer-line leak.

items.anchor_quote: it uses a near infrared laser and measures forward light scattering (30°)

items.location: Sec. IV Conclusion (future work, continues p.12)
items.anchor_quote: Future work should experimentally verify the applicability of the derived conversion factors.
items.summary: The authors call for experimental verification of the reference-to-smoke conversion factors and for measuring smoke size distributions and optical properties, combined with light scattering and absorption modelling, to explain detector differences and guide detector optimisation.
items.scope_notes: Forward-looking statement; (iii) size/optical characterization of smoke identified as a need.

items.anchor_quote: increased oxygen concentrations, partial gravity conditions and the presence of surface dust
items.summary: Missions beyond low Earth orbit will extend fire-safety conditions beyond NASA's five-decade experience to include long durations, dormancy, elevated oxygen, partial gravity and surface dust, all of which can affect fire safety system design.
items.scope_notes: (iv) frames elevated O2 / partial gravity / dust as new conditions; programmatic statement, not test data.

verification.note: Anchor on p.1; faithful.

items.location: Sec. I.A.2 Prior Detection and Suppression Systems
items.anchor_quote: both systems were adapted from terrestrial systems for spacecraft applications without verification
items.summary: Because no data existed on smoke particle sizes in low gravity or on reference fire sizes, Shuttle-era and later detection and suppression systems were adapted from terrestrial practice without verifying their effectiveness in low gravity; detectors were placed where ventilation ensures sampling, but the effect of the well-mixed cabin on detection threshold was not considered.
items.scope_notes: Historical design-basis statement.

verification.note: Anchor on p.2; faithful.

items.anchor_quote: with the ISS detectors more sensitive to larger particles while the Shuttle detectors
items.summary: The Shuttle and ISS smoke detectors had quite different particle-size sensitivities: the ISS detectors were more sensitive to larger particles, whereas the Shuttle detectors were designed to reject larger particles; the change followed available terrestrial technology rather than data on target fires.
items.scope_notes: (iii) particle-size coverage differs by detector; qualitative.

verification.note: Anchor on p.2; faithful.

items.anchor_quote: accumulation of hazardous compounds while alarm triggering is delayed
items.summary: In well-mixed spacecraft cabins smoke is diluted so roughly the whole volume must reach alarm level, and HEPA filtration removes smoke particles so concentration builds more slowly; filters may not remove hazardous gases, so toxic products can accumulate while the smoke alarm is delayed. Earlier modelling found that in many cases hazardous levels of products from multiple materials accumulated before the alarm threshold.
items.scope_notes: Based on cited modelling (Urban et al. ICES-2016-318), not on a measured missed alarm. Applies to microgravity, well-mixed, HEPA-filtered cabins.

verification.note: Anchor on p.3. Modelling basis confirmed (ref. 11 = Urban et al. ICES-2016-318). Correctly not labelled a missed alarm.

items.anchor_quote: the detection time could vary by over 2 minutes
items.summary: A cited ISS Destiny laboratory smoke-detection model (Brooker et al., 2007) showed that, for moderate smoke production rates, detection time could vary by more than two minutes; this paper does not state which parameter caused the variation.

numbers.meaning: variation in detection time in ISS Destiny model

items.scope_notes: Model result cited from 2007 work (ref. 10, 07ICES-113); the driver of the variation is not stated in this paper.

verification.note: Anchor and the 'over 2 minutes' value confirmed on p.3. The original summary attributed the variation to 'configuration' and the scope note to 'location'; this paper names neither. Both statements are now neutral.

original.summary: A cited ISS Destiny laboratory model (Brooker et al.) showed that, for moderate smoke production rates, detection time could vary by more than two minutes depending on configuration.
original.scope_notes: Model result cited from 2007 work; location dependence of detection.

items.anchor_quote: spacecraft fire detection thresholds should not be based on terrestrial levels or on other spacecraft
items.summary: The authors conclude that detection thresholds must be chosen for each vehicle volume and its air filtration and ventilation, with the interacting systems usually modelled in detail, rather than copied from terrestrial practice or other spacecraft.
items.scope_notes: Design recommendation derived from modelling studies.

verification.note: Anchor on p.3; faithful.

items.anchor_quote: the presence of buoyant flow will dominate the smoke transport even at Lunar g-levels
items.summary: Designing for reliable detection in both low gravity and on planetary surfaces is described as particularly challenging because buoyancy will dominate smoke transport even at lunar gravity, so detection design choices are expected to differ substantially between environments; more EVAs also bring more cabin dust and higher-oxygen environments.
items.scope_notes: (iv) partial gravity; expectation statement, no test data.

verification.note: Anchor on p.4; faithful.

items.location: Sec. II.C Fire Detection: Validation and Vehicle Scale Transport
items.anchor_quote: makes discrimination of smoke from dust particles difficult based simply on the aerosol concentration
items.summary: A space experiment found typical spacecraft smoke aerosols range roughly 100-500 nm (diameter of average mass); this size range makes it hard to distinguish smoke from dust using aerosol concentration alone. HEPA filtration by the ECLSS can substantially delay detection and allow hazardous products to build up, so detection design and alarm levels depend on the specific vehicle.

upper size of typical smoke (diameter of average mass)

items.location: Sec. II.D Fire Detection: Transfer Standard
items.anchor_quote: to characterize other expected smoke and nuisance aerosol sizes
items.summary: No database of reference spacecraft fires exists for qualifying detectors as terrestrial standards do; the authors propose transfer standards for manufacturers, which require more modelling and characterization of other expected smoke and nuisance aerosol sizes.
items.scope_notes: (ii)/(iii) nuisance-aerosol and smoke size characterization identified as open work (as of 2020).

verification.note: Anchor on p.5; faithful.

items.anchor_quote: HF HCl transport in a spacecraft needs further study
items.summary: Overheated-polymer tests gave initial estimates of HF, HCl and HCN yields and allowed evaluation of candidate gas instruments, but HF/HCl transport (adsorption onto spacecraft materials) needs further study, and more materials and fire sources must be characterized to decide which compounds to monitor.
items.scope_notes: Gas monitoring for contingency response, not primary smoke detection.

verification.note: Anchor on p.5; faithful (WSTF Li-ion laptop tests continue on p.6).

items.location: Sec. II.H Characterization of Lithium-ion Battery Fires
items.anchor_quote: The full impact of a Li-ion fire on a spacecraft cannot be reliably predicted
items.summary: Heat and hazardous-product release from a burning laptop in low gravity is too poorly known to predict the impact of a Li-ion battery fire; specific tests of heat release, product composition and spread risk, and of containment and extinguishment in low gravity, are needed.
items.scope_notes: Need statement; no detector performance data.

verification.note: Anchor on p.6; faithful.

items.anchor_quote: shutting off the spacecraft ventilation upon detecting a fire, are questionable or ineffective in partial-gravity
items.summary: Partial-gravity flammability is called a major gap: current low-gravity protocols such as NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 screening and shutting off ventilation upon fire detection may be questionable or ineffective in partial gravity, and no terrestrial facility exists for such experiments (a drop-tower, centrifuge rig and lunar-lander payload were being planned).

items.summary: NASA GRC is developing a fire detection system for partial and low gravity; a key design challenge is a low false-alarm rate, which requires discriminating combustion particles from cabin aerosol and lunar dust. Aerosol properties are measured in the GASP laboratory and cross-referenced to target detectors, and a CFD plume model is used for habitat smoke transport.

items.summary: The ASTM E662-type obscuration meter was linear with DRX PM2.5 from about 5 to 200 mg/m3, but its signal-to-noise ratio was low below about 5 mg/m3 (about 1%/m obscuration). The authors therefore used the DRX rather than obscuration as the concentration reference.

items.anchor_quote: multiple reference aerosols can be used for different smoke detectors and different smoke particles
items.summary: Because no single reference aerosol reproduced all detector-smoke combinations within +/-10%, the authors propose either using the Table 1 slope ratios as conversion factors or using different reference aerosols for different detectors and smoke types. They note that 5% DOS predicted CSP smoke responses within +/-20%.

items.anchor_quote: detection of a fire against nuisance aerosol sources is much simplified
items.summary: On Earth, buoyancy creates a concentrated, stratified smoke layer at the ceiling, which makes it much easier to detect a fire against nuisance aerosol sources. In a well-mixed spacecraft cabin the smoke is diluted instead, so the whole volume must reach the alarm threshold.
items.scope_notes: (ii) explains why the nuisance-aerosol discrimination margin is smaller in microgravity; qualitative design argument, no test data.

items.location: Sec. I.B.3 Vehicle Scale Fire Modeling
items.anchor_quote: there is no simple fire detection and suppression approach that will work for all
items.summary: Prior studies led the authors to conclude that, where flammable materials are present, no single fire detection and suppression approach works for all vehicle designs. Each vehicle must be modelled with its air circulation and filtration, avionics cooling and enclosures, stowage, volume, atmosphere composition and relief valves before detection and suppression requirements can be examined quantitatively.
items.scope_notes: Design-process recommendation from modelling studies (Dietrich et al., Urban et al.).

items.location: Sec. III.A Material Flammability, Ignition and Fire Growth
items.anchor_quote: conduct tests at elevated oxygen and reduced pressures that could be used on exploration
items.summary: As of 2020, Saffire IV-VI was planned to test larger samples for longer at the elevated-oxygen, reduced-pressure atmospheres proposed for exploration. The authors note that Saffire on Cygnus allows very limited changes to test conditions or samples between tests.
items.scope_notes: (iv) elevated O2 / reduced pressure; plan statement. Executed conditions are in ICES-2026-577 Table 1 (items 45, 51).

items.anchor_quote: results suggest that flammability limits determined in normal gravity may not be conservative
items.summary: Partial-gravity flammability data come only from thin fuels on low-gravity aircraft and from a centrifuge in the GRC 5.2 s drop tower. Both showed materials flammable at lower oxygen near lunar gravity than at 1 g or in microgravity, which suggests 1-g limits may not be conservative. The authors stress that the data set is very limited and that g-level effects on smoldering and deep-seated fires are an important area for future study.
items.scope_notes: (iv) partial gravity; flammability rather than detection, but relevant to which fires a lunar-habitat detector must see.

verification.note: Added by verifier; anchor checked on the cited page (whitespace-normalised).

items.anchor_quote: 2-sided samples show a 73% increase in the spread rate from an oxygen concentration increase
items.summary: Flame growth on PMMA in low gravity stayed linear rather than accelerating, even in high oxygen. For the two 2-sided samples, growth rate rose 73% for a 0.08 mol-fraction O2 increase despite a 45% pressure decrease (IV-2 to VI-3). For the two 1-sided samples, growth rate was unchanged for a 0.03 O2 increase with a 27% pressure decrease.
items.scope_notes: (iv) elevated O2 / reduced pressure. Based on four PMMA burns (two per comparison); fire growth, not detector response.

items.anchor_quote: The peak HRR hit 3 kW which is substantial for a small spacecraft.
items.summary: In SAFFIRE VI-3 the peak heat release rate reached about 3 kW, yet the temperature rise at the far-field diagnostics was only 0.5 °C. A peak of 77 °C was seen at the flow-unit outlet but dropped quickly through mixing and heat loss. Table 1 lists maximum temperature rises of 0.04-0.50 °C and pressure rises of 0.25-1.31 mbar at the FFD across the seven tests.

items.scope_notes: Vehicle-scale observation in this Cygnus configuration. The paper evaluates no heat or temperature detector; any implication for thermal detection is not drawn by the authors.

items.anchor_quote: the ISS where the smoke detectors are in front of air intakes
items.summary: The far-field diagnostics unit sat near the inlet of the Cygnus air circulation system, so it could stand in for where a smoke detector would trigger as circulation swept air to the intake. The authors liken this to ISS, where smoke detectors sit in front of air intakes.
items.detector: FFD (DustTrak DRX 8533; ionization sensor from a commercial smoke detector)
items.scope_notes: Explains the basis of the 2 mg/m3 surrogate-alarm analysis (item 51); a single sampling location, not a distributed detector network.

items.anchor_quote: the more important measure is the concentration of hazardous products at the time the fire
items.summary: The authors argue that hazardous-product concentration at the moment of detection matters more than peak values. Ideally the detection threshold should be set so that, for the expected fires in that spacecraft, detection comes early enough for the crew to respond effectively.
items.scope_notes: Framing for the time-to-alarm analysis; a general principle, not a specific threshold value.

items.location: Sec. III.A AGA (flight units); also p.6 EDU feature list
items.anchor_quote: implement gas alarm limit values unique to the spacecraft
items.summary: Of the fifteen flight AGAs, three are designated for Orion and use Orion-specific gas alarm limits. The EDU stage added audible and visible alarms and the ability to set separate ISS and Orion alarm limits (p.6), so the AGA alarms on gas concentration thresholds set per vehicle.
items.scope_notes: Gas-concentration alarms for contingency monitoring. The paper gives no alarm limit values and no fire-detection timing.

items.location: Sec. II.C Airborne Particles on ISS
items.anchor_quote: however there is no monitoring to verify whether they are met
items.summary: NASA sets maximum allowable concentrations for typical cabin dust on ISS, but the authors state that no monitoring verifies whether these limits are met. Knowledge of the cabin particle background comes from sample-return and real-time payload experiments.
items.scope_notes: (ii) background-aerosol knowledge gap relevant to false-alarm thresholds. Industry/academic authors.

items.location: Sec. II.B Spacecraft Smoke Particle Characterization
items.anchor_quote: All experiments incorporated the typical air velocity of the ventilation system on ISS
items.summary: The smoke-characterisation experiments behind the 100-1000 nm size range (the ISS experiment, matched ground tests and WSTF tests) all used the typical ISS ventilation air velocity. The authors expect this velocity to be similar in future vehicles.
items.scope_notes: (iii)/(iv) scope limitation: the size data come from ISS-like forced flow, oxidative pyrolysis only; partial-gravity or different-flow smoke is not covered by these data within the examined sources.

items.anchor_quote: based on many assumptions that cannot be substantiated
items.summary: The authors concede that their HALO alarm-threshold method rests on many assumptions that cannot be substantiated. They still consider it a reasonable way to tailor a threshold to HALO until a NASA standard exists.
items.scope_notes: Hedge on items 77-80. The approach is presented as interim guidance, not validated detection performance.

open_questions: SAFFIRE IV-VI: the 2020 plan (ICES-2020-173) promised low-g smoke size-distribution and transport measurements, but within the examined sources only DustTrak DRX mass concentration (PM fractions) and an ionization-chamber signal are reported; whether size distributions were published (e.g. ICES-2021-244) was not verified.

ICES-2026-577 Table 1 'time to alarm' values (92-1603 s) do not state the reference time point explicitly (the text says figures use a timeline starting ~10 min before ignition, and PMMA ignition durations differ); these values should not be compared across tests without clarifying the reference.

The 2 mg/m3 'alarm' in ICES-2026-577 is a surrogate threshold applied to a reference aerosol monitor, not a flight smoke detector; how a real ionization or photoelectric spacecraft detector would have responded in SAFFIRE IV-VI is not reported in the examined sources (the FFD ionization chamber signal is shown only as a figure).

HALO uses an ionization-style smoke detector (HALO threshold paper), while ICES-2025-361 notes ionization baseline current changes at low pressure; whether the HALO detector baseline was characterised across 9.5-10.2 psia (or at proposed lunar-surface ~8.2 psia atmospheres) is not documented in the examined sources.

Kapton/Teflon: post-SAME ground work (ICES-2020-340) quantified response slopes of ISS/STS/CSP detectors to Kapton and Teflon smoke but reported no alarm-time or missed-alarm outcomes; no post-2018 flight test of detectors with these smokes was found within the search log.

Smoke-vs-dust discrimination remains at prototype/preliminary stage within the examined sources (GRC 2026 poster with one fabric and LHS simulant; UDE polarimetric proof-of-principle with JSC-1AF; multi-angle 40/130 deg concept only seen as an abstract). No flight-qualified discriminating detector was found.

Partial-gravity smoke transport evidence found is computational only (COMSOL LES 2023 poster; NIST FDS laptop-fire plume 2026 poster); no partial-gravity smoke transport or detector experiment was found within the search log.

Role of gas sensing in early detection is unresolved across sources: the AGA is fielded as a contingency monitor, the GRC 2026 poster says trace gases are not considered an early signal, while modelling-based papers stress toxic gas accumulation before smoke alarm (ICES-2020-173, HALO paper).
The final HALO smoke-detector alarm threshold value is not stated in the examined excerpt; only the 3/5/7 mg/m3 exceedance analysis is shown.

Operational false-alarm frequency: the Shuttle figure (14 events) mixes BIT failures and false alarms, and ISS counts are stated to be unpublished; a quantitative false-alarm rate could not be established within the examined sources.

ICES-2020-340 Table 1: per unit DRX PM2.5, Kapton smoke gave the lowest ISS-scatter and obscuration response of six smokes (item 82). Whether this means later alarm for Kapton in a flight ISS detector is not tested in this paper. The DRX reference is itself size-dependent.

HALO threshold paper: the fresh full render has per-material extrapolated gas values (Tables 2-13, Appendix A) that are not in the stored excerpt, so they are not used as items. Storing the full text would allow quantitative Kapton/PTFE items.

ICES-2020-340: the authors' 'factor of over three' mineral-oil underestimate for the ISS scatter detector holds only for lamp wick and Teflon in their own Table 1c (Kapton 1.70, Nomex 1.97). Downstream text should not quote it as applying to all smokes.
